title: Coastline sculptures

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Contemporary art often inspires diverse and strong opinions, particularly when it is put in a public space. Built in 1889, the Eiffel Tower in Paris once ignited protest and disdain, but local people have grown to love it and tourists flock to see it from all over the world. Where the British coastline is concerned, people tend to be even more protective. Recent controversial creations include faceless figures near Liverpool, a concrete and glass tower near Portsmouth and plans for a skeleton steel church off the coast of Essex.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Antony Gormley's Another Place on Crosby Beach, near Liverpool, comprises 80-plus life-size statues looking out to sea, scattered over a mile of beach, stretching half a mile into the water. By placing something unexpected and removed from daily life in a public space, Gormley has transformed the scene. Created from casts of his own body, the intimate sculptures stand exposed on this public beach, and people respond to this in different ways. Some view the installation from a distance, in the setting of the coast, while others are drawn to individual figures, touching them and climbing on them, posing for photos. Prior to their installation, local and national media reported a raging debate. Some simply hated the look of the contemporary sculpture and wanted their beach back the way it had always been. Others feared that they themselves would be out of pocket, remembering how a glass tower in Portsmouth had experienced spiralling costs and left taxpayers with a bill for millions of pounds. The Gormley figures were intended to be temporary, having previously been shown in Germany, Norway and Belgium. Those who did not like the artwork were placated by the promise of a short stay. But in 2007, the Council granted permission for the installation, and Crosby Beach has never been so popular. Visitors come in coach loads in all weathers, not just for a few weeks in the summer. This boosts the local economy and helps raise the profile of Liverpool internationally as a centre of modern art.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In contrast, a single statue by Sam Holland was unveiled at Moelfre, Anglesey, in late 2004. This more traditional bronze statue depicts Die Evans, a member of the RNLI, a lifeboat charity that saves lives at sea. Evans was awarded a gold medal for his work for the charity and his statue was very well received by the local community. Unlike the static Gormley images, the Moelfre Statue is lifelike and animated, set at an angle to show character and movement. It is clear that this artist had real empathy for her subject: her grandfather was a good friend of Evans, and the young sculptor lives on a boat herself. The Moelfre Statue has a fine view across the picturesque bay towards the mountains and can be seen from the sea. Some sailors even use this landmark to guide them safely back into harbour. It has wide appeal too - many lifeboating people find it an inspirational focal point for celebrating all their comrades. While the unveiling of the Moelfre Statue was less controversial than the larger Gormley sculptures, some people are still concerned that the money should have been spent elsewhere, typically on local schools and hospitals rather than art. But the £40,000 cost was raised by the Moelfre Partnership specifically for the statue. Individuals and companies were inspired by the project and gave generously, producing the funds in just six months. Art is rarely universally applauded. But the vast majority do admire the Moelfre Statue and believe it draws people to the village throughout the year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Controversy is now raging over a planned installation off the coast of North Essex. The idea, by German architects Anne Niemann and Johannes Ingrisch, is to rebuild the church of medieval Walton, lost to the sea through coastal erosion. The Lost Church, to be constructed soon, will be made of stainless steel poles reaching towards the sky, half a mile from the coast. Local opinion is predictably split on this. Following a presentation by the architects, some who were against the project now support it wholeheartedly. Though concerns have been expressed about sea safety, there should be no added danger to vessels, as no yachts should come into such shallows. Also, any radar would pick up the massive steel structure straight away. One local seafarer admires the project artistically and thinks it will revitalise the area: 'This town needs something to make it as popular as it was in the 1950s and 1960s.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Time will tell, but it appears unlikely that the sculptures explored here pose a significant threat to public safety. They certainly give great joy and inspiration to thousands and bring much to their local communities. Contemporary art will always antagonise a minority, and intrusions into the natural environment of the sea will rile many more but, at best, sculpture adds successfully to the beauty and diversity of life.

subtitle: Loved or loathed, sculpture punctuates the British coastline, from installations (a form of sculpture that includes sound, movement or space) to traditional statues. Bethany Hope discusses what impact these artworks have had
